title: Decide What an Agent Can Do
subtitle: Map permissions to actions and keep approvals with the people who own them.

scenes.title: Set the permission boundary
scenes.body: Start with the specific task and its expected files.
scenes.narration: Take the model choice from the previous lesson and turn it into an access decision. Issue seventeen asks for a validator change and a test. Write down the two files, the working branch, and what you expect the assistant to produce. Keep production credentials and shared deployment systems outside this task. A manager can check the boundary by asking the author to explain every proposed permission against the ticket. Try it with the test file. Reading that file helps match the existing test style. Changing a pipeline falls outside the planned work.
scenes.code:
Task: issue #17, reject order quantity zero
Files: order_quantity.py, test_order_quantity.py
Branch: fix/reject-zero-quantity
scenes.result: Expected output: small diff and a regression test
scenes.focus: The task needs two repository files
scenes.action: Name the files and the working branch

scenes.title: Trace the data
scenes.body: Confirm what can travel and where it ends up.
scenes.narration: Sketch two boxes. The first is the client, such as Visual Studio Code or a CLI in the corporate Google Cloud workspace. The second is the model endpoint. Draw an arrow between them and label it with the selected code, ticket text, and synthetic test examples that may travel. Have the platform owner confirm the actual provider, endpoint, and retention terms for the approved setup. The machine that runs the client tells you one part of that story. If you cannot name the configured destination, keep the real source out of the request until the owner confirms it.
scenes.code:
VS Code or GCP workspace → configured endpoint
Record: provider, policy, retention and owner
Approved inputs: source examples and test data
scenes.result: Resolve an unknown endpoint before sharing code
scenes.focus: Client location and model endpoint differ
scenes.action: Record the destination and data class

scenes.title: Assign actions to roles
scenes.body: Set who may read, edit, test, publish, and review.
scenes.narration: Start with the permissions to read, edit, test, and publish. The assistant may read the scoped context and propose the patch on the working branch. The author inspects the edits and permits the specific test run in an approved environment. The author publishes the branch and opens the pull request with their own account. A different authorized teammate reviews it. Read the table from bottom to top as a check. If you see the same identity beside publish and final approval, identify who will perform the independent review before you start the pilot.
scenes.code:
Agent: read two files and propose scoped edits
Author: approve tests and publish the branch
Reviewer: inspect the PR and submit a decision
scenes.focus: Publishing and approval have distinct owners
scenes.action: Fill in the owner for each operation

scenes.title: Decide on an unexpected request
scenes.body: Keep the work inside the permissions it actually needs.
scenes.narration: Here is a permission prompt. The assistant asks to download a new test library. Pause and ask what would justify it. This repository already has tests in Python's standard library, so we have the capability needed for the zero case. Decline the network request and ask the assistant to follow the existing test style. Then inspect the diff for package files or dependency edits. If your team sees a repeated request of this kind, the platform lead can use the examples to clarify the task instructions or the permission defaults.
scenes.code:
Proposed action: download a test dependency
Agreed command: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests
scenes.action: Decline it and request the standard test

scenes.title: Read the human review evidence
scenes.body: Inspect what the check and independent review each prove.
scenes.narration: Now follow the evidence after publication. In the approved remote terminal, the reviewer uses GitHub CLI to read the diff and the checks for pull request forty-two. They confirm the zero regression, see that the checks passed, and submit a review with their own identity. For the manager walkthrough, read back that recorded decision and link it to issue seventeen. A passing check answers whether the test suite ran successfully. The review record answers who evaluated the change. Ask learners to point to one piece of evidence for each question.
scenes.code:
gh pr diff 42
gh pr checks 42
gh pr view 42 --json reviews
scenes.result: Evidence: separate reviewer and recorded decision
scenes.focus: PR #42 shows the check and reviewer
scenes.action: Open the diff, checks, and review record

scenes.title: Record the approval boundary
scenes.body: Document who decides when scope changes.
scenes.narration: Make the permission decision easy to look up. Save the task, the approved data class, where the assistant runs, the actions it can take, and who handles exceptions. If you later evaluate Claude Code or OpenCode in the corporate Google Cloud workspace, check which identities grant access to the shell, repository, and model. Their boundaries may differ from the editor workflow. Try one final exercise. A teammate asks to connect another data source. Who has to review that request? In this example, the platform lead checks the new destination and permission before approving use.
scenes.code:
Engineering lead: owns the pilot
Platform lead: controls data and permissions
Reviewer: evaluates the proposed change
scenes.result: Reassess before changing tools, data, or access
scenes.focus: New data, tools, or access trigger a review
scenes.action: Assign a named owner for exceptions
